title: Grade 4 Subtraction Word Problems: 3 Story Types + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 4 Subtraction Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master grade 4 subtraction word problems: take-away, compare and missing-part stories with large numbers and borrowing across zeros. Free quiz inside.
excerpt: A word problem does not tell you it is subtraction. Here are the three story types Grade 4 children meet, how to spot each one, and how to check the answer by adding back.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a question I gave a Class 4 group in Nagpur last year: a cricket stadium seats 12,450 people, and on match day 3,675 seats were empty — how many fans came? Almost every hand shot up to add. The word ‘empty’ had thrown them. The maths is easy once you see it is 12,450 − 3,675, but grade 4 subtraction word problems rarely wave a ‘minus’ flag. They hide the subtraction inside a story, and the child’s real job is to figure out what is being taken away, compared, or missing.

By Grade 4 the numbers get big too — four and five digits, often with borrowing across zeros. So there are two skills stacked on top of each other: reading the story correctly, and then subtracting large numbers without slips. Let me split the stories into the three types that cover almost everything a nine-year-old will meet.

The three types of subtraction story

Every subtraction word problem at this level is one of three shapes. Once a child can name the shape, choosing the operation stops being a guess.

1. Take-away (something is removed)

The classic. You start with an amount and part of it goes away — spent, sold, eaten, left the room. ‘A shopkeeper had 8,000 rupees and spent ₹2,750 on stock. How much is left?’ Signal words: spent, gave away, sold, used, left, remaining. You subtract the part that leaves from the whole.

2. Difference / compare (how much more or fewer)

Nothing is removed here — you are lining up two amounts and asking how far apart they are. ‘Anaya scored 9,340 points and Rahul scored 6,815. How many more did Anaya score?’ Signal words: more than, fewer than, taller, longer, difference between, how much bigger. This is the type children most often add by mistake, because the word ‘more’ feels like plus.

3. Missing part (the whole and one part are known)

You know the total and one piece, and the other piece is missing. ‘A school ordered 5,000 notebooks. If 3,240 have arrived, how many are still to come?’ Signal words: how many more are needed, still to come, the rest, remaining to reach. It looks like take-away, but the thinking is ‘whole minus known part’.

Take-awayHow much is left after some goesHad ₹8,000, spent ₹2,7508,000 − 2,750

Borrowing across zeros — the part that trips them up

The stadium sum, 12,450 − 3,675, needs borrowing in almost every column. The really painful ones have zeros in the top number, like 5,000 − 3,240. You cannot borrow from a zero directly, so the borrow has to travel left until it finds a digit to take from. I teach it as a chain: the 5 lends to the first 0, which passes it along, so the run of zeros all become 9 and the borrow finally reaches the ones column.

  • Line the numbers up by place value — ones under ones, thousands under thousands.
  • Work right to left, one column at a time.
  • When the top digit is smaller, borrow; if the neighbour is 0, keep moving left until you hit a non-zero digit.
  • Every 0 you pass on the way becomes a 9.
  • Never subtract the small digit from the big one just because it looks tidier — that is the single most common mistake I see.

Multi-step problems: subtraction as one move

Grade 4 also introduces problems where subtraction is only part of the answer. ‘A library had 6,200 books. It bought 1,450 more, then donated 900. How many now?’ That is one addition and one subtraction, in order. The trick is to do exactly one step at a time and write the in-between number down — 6,200 + 1,450 = 7,650, then 7,650 − 900 = 6,750. Children who try to hold both steps in their head are the ones who lose marks. Slow the hand down and the answer follows.

Write the sentence before you calculate

Before touching the digits, I make children say the whole sentence: ‘I need to find how many fans came, so I take the empty seats away from the total seats.’ Naming the operation out loud catches the ‘empty means minus’ type of trap far better than any keyword list.

Always check by adding back

Subtraction has a built-in self-check that addition does not: the answer plus the number you took away should rebuild the number you started with. For 12,450 − 3,675 = 8,775, test it with 8,775 + 3,675 — if that lands on 12,450, the subtraction is sound. This one habit turns a shaky guess into a confident answer, and it costs about fifteen seconds. Make it non-negotiable.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz built entirely from these three story types — take-away, compare, and missing part — with a couple of borrow-across-zero and multi-step problems mixed in. Let your child work each one on paper, name the story type, and check by adding back. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives dozens of story problems with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Subtraction Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight story problems covering take-away, compare and missing-part subtraction with large numbers. Name the type, work it on paper, then check by adding back.
quiz.about: Grade 4 subtraction word problems with numbers to 99,999

questions.q: A stadium seats 12,450 people. On match day 3,675 seats were empty. How many fans came?
questions.explanation: Empty seats are taken away from the total: 12,450 − 3,675 = 8,775. This is a take-away story hidden by the word ‘empty’.

questions.q: Anaya scored 9,340 points and Rahul scored 6,815. How many MORE did Anaya score?
questions.explanation: ‘How many more’ is a compare story — find the difference: 9,340 − 6,815 = 2,525. Check by adding back: 6,815 + 2,525 = 9,340.

questions.q: A school ordered 5,000 notebooks. So far 3,240 have arrived. How many are still to come?
questions.explanation: Whole minus known part: 5,000 − 3,240 = 1,760. Borrow across the zeros. Check: 1,760 + 3,240 = 5,000.

questions.q: A shopkeeper had ₹8,000 and spent ₹2,750 on stock. How much money is left?
A library had 6,200 books. It bought 1,450 more, then donated 900. How many books now?
questions.explanation: Two steps: 6,200 + 1,450 = 7,650, then 7,650 − 900 = 6,750. Do one step at a time.

questions.q: Which of these is a COMPARE (difference) word problem?
options: A tank held 3,000 L and 900 L drained out
Mount A is 4,200 m and Mount B is 3,650 m; how much taller is A?
5,000 tickets printed, 2,300 sold; how many left?
questions.explanation: Comparing two heights and asking ‘how much taller’ is a difference story. The others are take-away or missing-part.

questions.q: A factory made 15,000 bulbs. 2,340 were faulty and thrown away. How many good bulbs remained?
questions.explanation: Take-away: 15,000 − 2,340 = 12,660. The zeros in 15,000 mean you borrow across them. Check: 12,660 + 2,340 = 15,000.

questions.q: After you work out 24,000 − 8,650 = 15,350, how do you CHECK the answer?
options: Add 15,350 + 8,650 and see if you get 24,000
questions.explanation: Adding back is the self-check: the answer plus what you took away should rebuild the start. 15,350 + 8,650 = 24,000, so it is correct.

faq.q: How do I know a word problem is subtraction and not addition?
faq.a: Ask what the story is doing. If something is removed (spent, sold, left), two amounts are compared (how much more or taller), or one part of a known whole is missing, it is subtraction — even when the word ‘more’ appears. Naming the story type beats memorising keywords.

faq.q: Why do compare problems confuse Grade 4 children so often?
faq.a: Because they contain the word ‘more’, which children link to adding. But ‘how many more did Anaya score’ asks for the gap between two scores, which is a subtraction. Teaching the three story types by name fixes this faster than any keyword rule.

faq.q: What is the hardest part of large-number subtraction at this level?
faq.a: Borrowing across zeros, as in 5,000 − 3,240. You cannot borrow from a zero, so the borrow travels left until it reaches a non-zero digit, turning every 0 it passes into a 9. Slow, column-by-column work prevents most errors.

faq.q: How should my child check a subtraction answer?
faq.a: Add back. The answer plus the number that was subtracted should equal the number you started with. If 12,450 − 3,675 = 8,775, then 8,775 + 3,675 must return 12,450. It takes seconds and catches nearly every slip.
